## Waves
$$
\begin{align}
k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \\
\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi \nu \\
 \frac{k\lambda}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2 }
\end{align}
$$
So adding a translation of $\frac{\lambda}{4}$ to $x$ gives 
$$
\begin{align}
\sin\left( k\left( x+\frac{\lambda}{4}\right) - \omega t \right) = \cos(kx-\omega t)
\end{align}
$$

Maxwell's equation for electric field in free space:

$$
\begin{align}
\frac{ \partial^{2}\mathcal{E}   }{ \partial x^{2} } - \frac{1}{c^{2}} \frac{ \partial^{2} \mathcal{E}  }{ \partial t^{2} } = 0 
\end{align}
$$


This looks like the diff EQ that we got when we rearranged the Schrödinger eq, which makes sense because both describe wave motion. 

The acceleration of the wave in space is related to the acceleration in time. Units cancel with $c$. 

Cos and Sine are solutions to maxwell's eq. if $\omega=kc$.
$k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}, \omega= \frac{2\pi}{T}$
so
$\frac{2\pi}{T}= \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}c \implies \frac{\lambda}{T}= c, \lambda \nu=c$

In a medium with index of refraction $n$, the speed of light becomes $\frac{c}{n}$. The frequency of the light stays the same, so the wavelength must decrease to compensate. It is traveling slower but oscillating the same speed, so the peaks would be closer to each other in space.

## Photons

If we take a photograph with vanishingly small amounts of light to activate the reaction, instead of decreasing the image uniformly we end up with stark spots of light. This is counter to the wave behavior, and is more like small particles hitting at one spot or another. 

*What determines the behavior for wave-particle duality? What systems do we observe one/the other/ both?*

### Compton scattering
If you shine light on a block of carbon, you would expect the electrons to have a system response to the light, and have the same steady state frequency. However, we also see a secondary dominant frequency that depends on the scattering angle. The photon bounces off the electron (and that bounces the other way).

The shift in wavelength is $\frac{h}{mc}$, where $h$ is plank's constant, and $m$ is the mass of the object (i.e. electron).
